description: Original InterviewRoom challenge catalog for hackathon demos.

challenges.title: Minimum Meeting Rooms
challenges.prompt: Given a list of calendar events with start and end times, determine the minimum number of meeting rooms required so that no meetings overlap in the same room.
examples: Events from nine to ten thirty, nine thirty to eleven, and eleven to noon require two rooms.
Events from nine to ten and ten to eleven can reuse one room if an event ending at ten does not overlap an event starting at ten.
constraints: The input may be unsorted.
Start times are earlier than end times.
Back-to-back events do not overlap.
The candidate may choose any reasonable representation for times.
interviewer_notes: Look for clarification about interval boundaries.
Look for sorting by start time or separate sorted start and end times.
Look for a heap of active meeting end times or an equivalent sweep.
Ask for time and space complexity before wrapping up.
hints: Think about processing the meetings in chronological order.
At any start time, only meetings that have not ended still need rooms.
A min heap of end times is one compact way to track active meetings.

challenges.title: First Unique Visitor
challenges.prompt: Given a stream or list of visitor identifiers in arrival order, return the first identifier that appears exactly once. If every identifier repeats, return no result.
examples: For visitors ava, ben, ava, cara, ben, the first unique visitor is cara.
For visitors kai, kai, noah, noah, there is no unique visitor.
constraints: Visitor identifiers are strings.
The input can be empty.
The candidate may solve for a finite list first, then discuss a streaming version.
Preserving original arrival order matters.
interviewer_notes: Look for a hash map from identifier to count.
Look for a second pass through the original order.
For a streaming follow-up, discuss queue plus counts or linked structure tradeoffs.
Ask how the solution changes if the stream is very large.
hints: Separate counting from preserving order.
A hash map can tell you whether a visitor is unique.
A second pass can find the earliest identifier whose count is one.

challenges.title: Support Ticket SLA
challenges.prompt: Design a function that receives support tickets with creation times, priority levels, and estimated handling times, then returns the order in which an agent should process them to minimize missed service-level deadlines.
examples: A high-priority ticket due in ten minutes should usually be handled before a low-priority ticket due tomorrow.
If two tickets have the same deadline risk, the earlier created ticket should come first.
constraints: Each ticket has an id, creation time, priority, estimated handling time, and deadline.
Priorities are high, medium, or low.
The first version can assume one support agent.
The candidate should state how ties are resolved.
interviewer_notes: Look for a clear ranking strategy and tie breakers.
Probe whether priority or deadline should dominate.
Ask how the design changes for multiple agents.
Ask what data structure would support live ticket insertion.
hints: Try defining a risk score or ordering key before coding.
Deadlines and estimated handling time can reveal which ticket is most urgent.
A priority queue can keep the next best ticket available as new tickets arrive.

challenges.title: Comment Thread Depth
challenges.prompt: Given a list of comments where each comment has an id and an optional parent id, compute the maximum nesting depth of the thread. Invalid parent references should not crash the program.
examples: A root comment with two direct replies has depth two.
A root comment, a reply, and a reply to that reply has depth three.
constraints: The comments may arrive in any order.
Some parent ids may be missing.
A robust solution should avoid infinite loops if bad data creates a cycle.
There may be multiple root comments.
interviewer_notes: Look for building an adjacency list or parent lookup.
Ask how the candidate handles missing parents.
Probe cycle detection and recursion depth concerns.
Ask for complexity in terms of comments and parent links.
hints: Start by grouping comments by parent id.
Depth-first search from each root is one natural approach.
A visited or visiting set can protect against cycles.

challenges.title: Shopping Cart Promotions
challenges.prompt: Implement a checkout helper that applies a buy-two-get-one-free promotion to a shopping cart. For every three items in the same product category, the cheapest one should be free.
examples: Three books priced ten, eight, and six make the six dollar book free.
Six snacks in one category should create two free items, each chosen to maximize the customer's discount.
constraints: Promotions apply within the same product category only.
The input may contain multiple categories.
Prices are non-negative decimal values.
The candidate should avoid mutating the original cart unless they state that choice.
interviewer_notes: Look for grouping by category before applying discounts.
Look for sorting prices in descending order to maximize the discount.
Ask about decimal money handling.
Probe edge cases such as fewer than three items and zero-priced items.
hints: Handle one category at a time.
Think about which items should be grouped together to maximize the discount.
Sorting each category's prices can make the free-item positions clear.

challenges.title: Frontend Filter State
challenges.prompt: Design a product search page state model with text search, category filters, sorting, and pagination. Explain how the UI state should sync with the URL so users can share a filtered view.
examples: A user searches for headphones, filters to audio, sorts by rating, and shares the URL.
Changing the search text should reset pagination back to the first page.
constraints: The user should be able to use the browser back button naturally.
The state should support multiple selected categories.
The search box may debounce network requests.
The candidate can describe components and data flow instead of writing full UI code.
interviewer_notes: Look for clear separation between view state and server query parameters.
Ask what belongs in the URL versus local component state.
Probe race conditions from debounced searches.
Ask how the candidate would test the behavior.
hints: Start by listing the state fields and who owns them.
Shareable state usually belongs in the URL.
Debouncing changes when requests fire, not what the canonical filter state is.

challenges.title: Undo Redo Editor
challenges.prompt: Design a small text editor history system that supports applying edits, undo, and redo. After a new edit is applied, redo history should be cleared.
examples: Typing A, typing B, then undo should return the document to A.
Typing A, undo, then typing C should make redo unavailable.
constraints: An edit can be represented as a complete document snapshot or as an operation.
The first version can use strings for document contents.
Undo on the initial state should be safe.
The candidate should discuss the memory tradeoff of snapshots versus operations.
interviewer_notes: Look for two-stack reasoning.
Ask when redo history should be invalidated.
Probe memory and performance tradeoffs.
Ask how this design changes for collaborative editing.
hints: One stack can hold past states and one can hold undone future states.
Undo moves state in one direction; redo moves it back.
A brand-new edit should discard the future states.

challenges.title: Grid Delivery Zones
challenges.prompt: Given a city grid where open cells represent deliverable addresses and blocked cells represent unavailable areas, count how many separate delivery zones exist.
examples: A grid with two disconnected groups of open cells has two delivery zones.
Open cells connected diagonally only should be considered separate unless the candidate explicitly chooses diagonal movement.
constraints: The grid can be empty.
Connectivity should be defined using up, down, left, and right neighbors.
The candidate may mutate a copy of the grid or use a visited set.
The solution should avoid revisiting the same cell repeatedly.
interviewer_notes: Look for a traversal from each unvisited open cell.
Ask the candidate to define adjacency.
Probe empty grid and jagged row edge cases.
Ask for time and space complexity in terms of rows and columns.
hints: Treat each open cell as a node in a graph.
Starting a search from an unvisited open cell discovers one whole zone.
A visited set prevents double counting.
